meta.framing: The client asked for one thing: the best decision for the property and for the owner as an individual, preserving wealth while keeping risk manageable. That means the answer must be conditional on facts not yet supplied, so it is expressed as a ranked strategy plus explicit decision triggers.
meta.scoring_note: Scores are analyst judgments (1-5) built on the verified data and the model output. They are not measurements. Weights: wealth preservation 35%, growth 25%, execution risk 20%, liquidity 10%, tax efficiency 10%.

options.name: Sell now (2026-2027) and 1031-exchange into diversified net lease
options.summary: Capture today's pricing before the short-WALT discount appears, defer gain with a Section 1031 exchange, and replace one tenant and one parcel with several.
pros: Removes single-tenant, single-parcel, single-metro concentration - the largest risk in the file (RK20).
Section 1031 defers the tax that would otherwise consume a large share of proceeds (S16, RK19).
Verified net-lease deployment benchmark is 7.3% (S10) versus the 6.97% reinvestment yield the base case needs to match holding - a thin but positive margin.
Avoids the short-WALT buyer pool problem entirely (RK05).
cons: Gives up a 2% Prop 13 assessment cap in a 3.6% CPI environment (S6, S1) - a real, permanent benefit that is not transferable.
Forfeits the option value of a market-rent reset at 2030-2035 if contract rent is below market (RK03).
Execution risk: 45/180-day exchange identification rules (S16) and a 3.5%+ cost stack including city/county transfer taxes (S7, S8).
If the asset is actually worth more than the benchmark suggests, selling now may leave value on the table.

options.name: Negotiate an early extension with a rent reset, then sell with a long WALT
options.summary: Use the 2030-2035 expiry as leverage: trade the tenant a 10-20 year extension for a market rent reset and a credit guaranty, then sell the re-priced asset into the deepest possible buyer pool.
pros: Creates the value that D1 gives up: a market reset plus a long lease is the highest-priced version of this asset (RK03, RK05).
The tenant has structural incentive - its franchise term is 20 years and it reprices renewals to market anyway (S9).
Selling after the reset removes the short-WALT discount and attracts 1031 buyers who need term.
Keeps the 2% assessment cap (S6) while the extension is negotiated.
cons: Requires the tenant to cooperate; a franchisee facing a $20/hour fast-food wage floor (S5) and a 3.8% AUV decline (S9) may not be able to absorb a higher rent.
Two-step execution (negotiate, then market) with timing risk on rates (S11).
Extending a lease you then sell can be seen by buyers as a captured premium rather than a gift.

options.name: Hold to expiry, renew at market, keep the asset
options.summary: Do nothing until the option window, then reprice at market and continue collecting NNN rent with an inflation-capped tax basis.
pros: Model base case: holding beats selling and reinvesting at the Treasury rate by about $1.36M of 2040 wealth, and beats it in every scenario tested.
Beats selling and reinvesting at the 7.3% net-lease benchmark in the bull case by about $0.43M (model output).
No transaction cost, no tax event, no reinvestment risk, and the Prop 13 basis persists (S6).
Zero action required until the option window opens - the cheapest path administratively.
cons: In the bear case, holding loses about $0.69M versus selling and reinvesting at the net-lease benchmark.
Concentration risk compounds over 6-14 more years (RK20).
Wildfire, earthquake and insurance shocks are unhedged by diversification (RK12, RK13, RK15).
Leaves the owner exposed to a single franchisee's credit (RK02).

options.name: Hybrid: extend 5 years now at a reset rent, keep a 2030-2035 sale window
options.summary: Take a short extension with a fair-market reset and a strengthened guaranty, then decide at the new expiration with full information and a re-priced asset.
pros: Locks in a rent reset (the model needs only +7.1% uplift to beat selling into the net-lease benchmark) while preserving the sale option.
Avoids both the short-WALT discount and the permanent loss of the Prop 13 basis.
Buys time to complete parcel-level hazard and insurance work that is currently unverified (M82-M85).
Limits downside: a 5-year extension is short enough to reprice again in a better market.
cons: A short extension still leaves a short WALT at the next decision point.
Requires tenant consent and a guaranty the franchisee may not be able to give.
Splits the difference on every axis - the classic risk of a compromise.

recommendation.headline: Do not choose between 'sell' and 'renew' as a slogan. Run a sequenced plan: strengthen the lease now, price the asset in 2027-2028, and sell into a 1031 exchange only if pricing and the replacement yield clear explicit thresholds.
why: The model shows the decision is not dominated by either side. Base case: selling and reinvesting at the verified 7.3% net-lease benchmark beats holding by about $0.25M of 2040 wealth; holding beats selling and reinvesting at the Treasury rate by about $1.36M. The answer turns on the reinvestment yield the owner can actually achieve - the breakeven is 6.97%.

Because the margin is thin, the highest-value action is not to sell or to hold, but to change the asset: secure a market-rent reset and a longer term. That is the only path that improves both the sell price and the hold economics.

Everything that could move the answer by more than the thin margin is a fact the owner has not yet supplied: actual rent, exact expiry, basis, debt, and the parcel's hazard classification. So the plan below is trigger-based, not a blind instruction.

plan.action: Assemble the twelve missing documents (P01-P12). Nothing else is decision-grade until rent, expiry date, basis and debt are known.
Order parcel-level hazard and insurance verification: FEMA flood zone, CAL FIRE/LACoFD FHSZ, CGS seismic and liquefaction, and a current property quote (closes M82-M85).
Open the extension conversation with the franchisee. Ask for a fair-market reset with a floor, a 10-year extension, and a guaranty. Model any offer against the +7.1% uplift threshold.
Obtain a broker opinion of value and an appraisal. If the implied cap rate is at or below 6.00%, sell. If it is above 7.00%, hold and extend instead (see the sensitivity grid).
Engage a qualified intermediary before listing, identify replacement property inside 45 days, close inside 180 days, and buy at least three properties to break the concentration (S16).
Build a reserve equal to 12 months of NOI against the earthquake/wildfire/insurance tail (RK12, RK13, RK15), and re-test the decision every 24 months.

decision_triggers.trigger: Appraisal implies a cap rate of 6.00% or lower
decision_triggers.action: Sell, and exchange into diversified net lease.

decision_triggers.trigger: Appraisal implies a cap rate above 7.00%
decision_triggers.action: Hold, extend, and re-test in 24 months.

decision_triggers.trigger: Tenant will sign a 10-year extension at market with a guaranty
decision_triggers.action: Take it, then market the asset with long WALT (D2).

decision_triggers.trigger: Tenant refuses any reset and the option rent is fixed at a below-market number
decision_triggers.action: Do not extend. Market the asset before the short-WALT discount deepens (D1).

decision_triggers.trigger: Insurance quote exceeds 1.5% of value or coverage is unavailable
decision_triggers.action: Treat as a sell trigger regardless of cap rate.

decision_triggers.trigger: Parcel sits in a very-high fire hazard zone or a mapped liquefaction zone
decision_triggers.action: Reduce the hold bias; obtain engineering and insurance clarity before any extension.

individual_owner_layer: Wealth preservation first: a single-tenant, single-parcel, single-metro asset worth roughly $2.0M-$2.7M at the benchmark rent is a concentrated position. Diversification is the only free risk reduction available, and a 1031 exchange is the tax-efficient way to get it (S16).

Do not sell for the sake of selling: at the benchmark rent the asset prices below the $5.4M Measure ULA threshold, so the 4%/5.5% surtax does not bite, and the transfer-tax cost stack is about 0.56% plus brokerage (S7, S8). The friction is real but not disqualifying.
Keep the option alive: a 5-year extension preserves both the tax basis (S6) and the sale option, which is why D4 ranks second rather than last.

Reserve, then reinvest: whatever the decision, hold a 12-month NOI reserve outside the property. Every black-swan scenario in the register ends in a liquidity problem before it ends in a valuation problem.
